Q1.answer: The paper investigates whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent statistics (rolling-window normalization, RWN) reduces forecasting error when the level of the time series shifts after training, compared to using fixed training-set statistics.

Q2.answer: Forecasters deployed on streaming data (e.g., electricity demand) encounter level shifts. Standard practice normalizes with training data statistics, which may cause error after a shift. It matters because the post-shift error could stem from the normalization itself rather than model capacity.
Q2.missing: No citation or evidence given for prevalence of level shifts in deployed load forecasting; marked [CITATION NEEDED].

Q3.answer: The gap is that it is unknown whether RWN reduces error under level shift without harming unshifted accuracy, and how much of any gain depends on continued adaptation of the normalization statistics. Existing pipelines use fixed training statistics; the contribution of normalization vs. model capacity to post-shift error has not been separated.
Q3.missing: No literature review or citations provided to substantiate what prior work has/has not done; two [CITATION NEEDED] placeholders.

Q4.answer: Generated a synthetic hourly series (SynthLoad) with daily/weekly cycles and Gaussian noise. Added level shifts of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 training standard deviations. Compared three normalization methods: Baseline (training mean/std), RWN (mean/std of most recent 48 steps), RWN-fixed (freeze statistics after first 48 post-shift steps). All used the same MLP, same training budget, 5 random seeds. Measured MAE.

Q5.answer: To isolate the effect of normalization from model capacity, the model architecture and training budget were held fixed. RWN uses a 48-step window (two days of hourly data) to capture recent level. RWN-fixed ablation tests dependence on continued adaptation. Synthetic data enables controlled shift magnitudes.
Q5.missing: No justification for the specific 48-step window length or why an MLP was chosen over other forecasters.

Q6.answer: MAE evaluation on SynthLoad across shift magnitudes s ∈ {0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8} for Baseline and RWN (5 seeds each). Single ablation: RWN-fixed at s=0.6 only. One model (MLP), one synthetic generator, one window length (48).

Q8.answer: RWN substantially reduces error under moderate level shifts (s=0.2–0.6) without harming accuracy when there is no shift (s=0.0). Part of the gain depends on continued adaptation: at s=0.6, RWN-fixed (0.518) is between Baseline (0.641) and RWN (0.452). At large shift (s=0.8), RWN provides minimal benefit.

Q9.answer: Does not establish: generality to real data (only SynthLoad), other models (only one MLP), other shift types (only level shifts), optimal window length (only 48 tested), statistical significance of differences (only ±std across 5 seeds), performance at other forecast horizons, or whether RWN-fixed would show similar partial adaptation at other shift magnitudes (only tested at s=0.6).

Q10.answer: Empirical evaluation of rolling-window normalization vs. training-statistics normalization under controlled level shifts, with an ablation (RWN-fixed) showing that part of the benefit comes from continued adaptation of the normalization statistics.

Q11.answer: Synthetic data only; single model (MLP); only level shifts tested; fixed window length (48); RWN-fixed ablation only at s=0.6; no statistical significance testing; no real-data validation; no comparison to other adaptation methods.

Q12.answer: Rolling-window normalization (using the most recent 48 steps) can substantially reduce forecasting error under moderate level shifts without hurting performance when there's no shift, and roughly half the benefit at s=0.6 comes from continued adaptation of the normalization statistics.

objective_discrepancies: Objective states the paper should show 'how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt those statistics' — but RWN-fixed is only evaluated at s=0.6, so the paper only answers this for one shift magnitude, not as a general function of shift size.

Objective says 'A reader should come away knowing what was tested, what was found, and where the finding stops' — the paper succeeds on 'what was tested' and 'what was found' (via clear limitations), but the 'where the finding stops' is only partially addressed (missing: model generality, real data, other shift types, window length sensitivity).
